steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Stress is the force applied to rock; strain is the resulting deformation

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Brittle deformation: rocks fracture under stress, producing joints, faults and fractures (dominant at shallow depths, low temperature, fast strain rate)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Ductile deformation: rocks bend or flow under stress, producing folds and cleavage (dominant at depth, high temperature, slow strain rate)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Normal faults form under tension: the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What determines whether a rock deforms in a brittle or ductile manner? | Q: How does a normal fault differ from a reverse fault? | Q: What is the difference between a joint and a fault?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Temperature, pressure (depth), strain rate and rock type. High temperature and pressure (great depth) favour ductile deformation (folding). A reverse fault forms under compression, the hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall. | A joint is a fracture with no movement along it. A fault is a fracture where the rock blocks have moved relative to each other.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Brittle vs ductile: depth and temperature are the key controls Normal fault = tension (hanging wall down); Reverse fault = compression (hanging wall up) Joints have NO movement; faults HAVE movement Stress is the cause; strain is the effect
